lead: With variable coefficients, the multipliers in front of y″, y′ and y change with x. You cannot write e^{mx} and get a polynomial. The chapter gives a practical route: if one nonzero solution is known, one integration supplies the second. The Wronskian then confirms independence, and variation of parameters gives the particular integral. This is used when a model has drifting damping, a variable spring, or a coefficient like 1/x, and when a textbook asks for a second solution after handing you the first.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for independence and the Wronskian, Chapter 2.5 for the particular-integral formula, and confident integration by substitution and parts.

sections.h3: Put it in standard form first

blocks.text: Start with a₀(x)y″ + a₁(x)y′ + a₂(x)y = f(x). At every x where a₀(x) ≠ 0, divide the whole equation by a₀(x). This gives the standard form y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = R(x). Here P = a₁/a₀, Q = a₂/a₀ and R = f/a₀. All formulas below use this form.

Suppose one nonzero solution y₁ of the homogeneous equation y″ + P y′ + Q y = 0 is known. Put y = v(x)y₁(x). Substitute y, y′, y″. The terms containing v cancel because y₁ solves the homogeneous equation. What remains is y₁v″ + (2y₁′ + P y₁)v′ = 0. Let w = v′. Then w′/w = −(2y₁′/y₁ + P). Integrate: w = C e<sup>−∫P dx</sup>/y₁². Integrate again to get v. The second solution is y₂ = y₁ ∫ e<sup>−∫P dx</sup>/y₁² dx. The constant C only multiplies y₂ by a number, so ignore it.
y₂ = y₁ ∫ e<sup>−∫P dx</sup> / y₁² dx
blocks.where: y₁ is the known nonzero solution; P is the coefficient of y′ in standard form; the inner ∫P dx is any antiderivative; the outer integral gives v.

items: Divide by a₀(x) before reading P.
Check that y₁ solves the homogeneous equation.
Compute e<sup>−∫P dx</sup> and divide by y₁².
Integrate once, multiply by y₁, and drop constant multiples.

blocks.text: Abel's identity states W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂ = W₀ e−∫P dx. W₀ is the value of the Wronskian at any convenient point; e−∫P dx is the same integrating factor as above. If W₀ ≠ 0, then W ≠ 0 everywhere, and y₁, y₂ are independent. If W₀ = 0, the two solutions are dependent; y₂ is not a second solution. See Chapter 2.3.

For the nonhomogeneous equation y″ + P y′ + Q y = R, the complementary function is y_c = C₁y₁ + C₂y₂. Variation of parameters, from Chapter 2.5, sets y_p = u₁y₁ + u₂y₂. Impose u₁′y₁ + u₂′y₂ = 0 and u₁′y₁′ + u₂′y₂′ = R. Solve the two linear equations: u₁′ = −y₂R/W and u₂′ = y₁R/W. Integrate to get u₁, u₂, then y_p. The full solution is y = C₁y₁ + C₂y₂ + y_p. The W in the denominator is the Wronskian of y₁ and y₂. If R = 0, then u₁′ = u₂′ = 0 and y_p = 0, as expected.

blocks.where: W is the Wronskian of y₁ and y₂; R is the right-hand side after standard form; y_p = u₁y₁ + u₂y₂.

blocks.text: Most variable-coefficient equations do not have elementary closed forms. Two families do. A Cauchy-Euler equation has the shape x²y″ + a x y′ + b y = f(x); the substitution x = e^t, or t = ln x, turns it into a constant-coefficient equation. See Chapter 2.6. Some other equations become constant-coefficient after a suitable substitution; check for that before integrating. If no substitution works, use a power series about an ordinary point or a regular singular point, which is Unit 3. For numbers rather than formulas, use a numerical method such as fourth-order Runge-Kutta or finite differences. In practice, reduction of order is used when a solver or a symmetry argument has already produced one solution, and you need the second to write the general solution. Such equations are common when a material property changes with position.

figure.caption: One solution plus one integration gives the second; the Wronskian checks independence, and variation of parameters adds the particular integral.

spec.title: One solution buys the second
spec.aria: A flow from one known solution through reduction of order to the second solution, then to the Wronskian, then to variation of parameters for the particular integral.

examples.question: Given that y₁ = x is a nonzero solution of x²y″ + x y′ − y = 0, find a second independent solution. Hence solve x²y″ + x y′ − y = x² subject to y(1) = 1 and y′(1) = 0, and evaluate y(2).
steps: Divide by x² on an interval with x > 0: y″ + (1/x)y′ − (1/x²)y = 0. So P = 1/x, Q = −1/x², and for the full equation R = x²/x² = 1.
Compute ∫P dx = ln x, so e<sup>−∫P dx</sup> = e<sup>−ln x</sup> = 1/x.
Use reduction of order: y₂ = x∫ (1/x)/x² dx = x∫ x⁻³ dx = x(−1/(2x²)) = −1/(2x). Drop the constant −1/2 and take y₂ = 1/x.
For the full equation, R = 1 and W = −2/x. Then u₁′ = −(1/x)(1)/(−2/x) = 1/2, so u₁ = x/2. Also u₂′ = x(1)/(−2/x) = −x²/2, so u₂ = −x³/6.
Thus y_p = (x/2)x + (−x³/6)(1/x) = x²/2 − x²/6 = x²/3. Check: y_p″ = 2/3 and y_p′ = 2x/3, so x²(2/3) + x(2x/3) − x²/3 = x².
The general solution is y = C₁x + C₂/x + x²/3.
Use y(1) = 1: C₁ + C₂ + 1/3 = 1, so C₁ + C₂ = 2/3. Use y′(1) = 0 with y′ = C₁ − C₂/x² + 2x/3: C₁ − C₂ + 2/3 = 0, so C₁ − C₂ = −2/3. Solve: C₁ = 0 and C₂ = 2/3.
examples.answer: The second solution is y₂ = 1/x; the initial value problem has y = (2/3)(1/x) + x²/3, so y(2) = 5/3 ≈ 1.667.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction
s = Fraction(1, 1) - Fraction(1, 3)
d = -Fraction(2, 3)
C1 = (s + d) / 2
C2 = (s - d) / 2
y = C1 * 2 + C2 / 2 + 4 / 3
print(float(C1))
print(float(C2))
print(float(y))

traps: Dividing by a₀ is not optional: in a₀y″ + a₁y′ + a₂y = f, P = a₁/a₀, not a₁.
Using a y₁ that solves a different equation; the reduction formula assumes y₁ solves the homogeneous part.
Sign slip in Abel's identity: W = W₀e<sup>−∫P dx</sup>; the minus is part of the exponent.
Swapping the signs in variation of parameters: u₁′ = −y₂R/W and u₂′ = +y₁R/W.
Keeping an extra constant in y₂; constant multiples of y₂ are still the same independent solution, so drop them.

quiz.q: State the standard form used for reduction of order and name P, Q, R.
quiz.a: y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = R(x), with P = a₁/a₀, Q = a₂/a₀ and R = f/a₀ after dividing a₀y″ + a₁y′ + a₂y = f by a₀.

quiz.q: Why does the substitution y = v y₁ lower the order of the homogeneous equation?
quiz.a: Because y₁ solves the homogeneous equation, all terms containing v cancel. Only v″ and v′ remain, so setting w = v′ gives a first-order equation for w.

quiz.q: If y₁ = x² solves x²y″ − 3xy′ + 4y = 0, find a second independent solution.
quiz.a: Standard form has P = −3/x and e<sup>−∫P dx</sup> = x³. Then y₂ = x²∫ x³/x⁴ dx = x²∫ (1/x) dx = x² ln x.

quiz.q: Abel's identity gives W = W₀e<sup>−∫P dx</sup>. What does W₀ = 0 imply for two solutions of the same second-order linear ODE?
quiz.a: It implies W = 0 everywhere, so the two solutions are dependent. The second solution is a constant multiple of the first, not a new independent solution.

quiz.q: For y″ + (1/x)y′ − (1/x²)y = 1 with y₁ = x and y₂ = 1/x, write u₁′ and u₂′ for variation of parameters.
Why does the substitution x = e^t help a Cauchy-Euler equation?
quiz.a: It turns powers of x multiplying derivatives into constant coefficients, so the equation becomes a constant-coefficient linear ODE in t.

beyond: Not for the exam. In research, variable-coefficient second-order equations appear in wave propagation through layered media and in option pricing with local volatility. Search for reduction of order, Abel's identity, and Sturm-Liouville theory. The Sturm-Liouville form puts many physical equations into a self-adjoint shape, where eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenfunctions do the work. Numerical solvers such as Runge-Kutta 4 are the practical fallback when no closed form exists.
